rv.q: Nicholas Hytner's bracing production ran in the West End in 2024 with the same four actors in the main roles, and they mostly work together as a smooth machine.
It's a credit to the direction of Nicholas Hytner that Lithgow's titanic performance doesn't unbalance the show.
What we have here is, in essence, a furiously verbose debate play revolving around two very prescient questions.
I found Lithgow's performance a fascinating study in monstrosity, but I found myself more engaged by the conversations I've had since seeing 'Giant'
It is the tragedy of someone who had brains, heart, and imagination willfully becoming smaller.
It’s Lithgow’s ability to be quiet and sweet and seconds later booming and scary that makes us squirm in our seats over our own feelings toward the writer.
You won’t see a more powerful play this season, or a more important one.
Giant, thrilling and abrasive, is full of rewards.

Giant is not just a dramatization of one man’s descent into antisemitism, but a tragedy depicting the failure of the fight against antisemitism, which has mostly been a triumph of manners over genuine persuasion—and the taboo is cracking.
It is smart, timely, and anchored by a commanding central performance, but ultimately more compelling in its questions than in its dramatic execution.
But the quibbles hardly matter considering Lithgow’s towering performance, which blends warmth and ugliness in fascinating fashion.
But Rosenblatt is a brave and intelligent playwright willing to take on a subject that no one else seems willing to touch.

For all its dramatic pleasures and gestures towards nuance, Giant winds up feeling like the latest example of a type of weaponized censorship that deems any criticism of governments as human-scale hate speech.
Lithgow delivers a real feast for theatergoers.
He’s horrifying, fascinating, and devastating all at once.
What makes the work sing is its refusal to resort to caricature, humanizing Dahl through his fiancée
